blocks.title: Seismometer
blocks.text: A seismometer is an instrument that responds to any movement of the rocks under the ground, or vibration caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and explosions. It detects earthquakes by using electromagnetic induction to convert ground motion into electrical signals.

Typically a seismometer includes a weight suspended by a spring. When an earthquake occurs, the ground moves but the weight tends to stay stationary because of its inertia. This results in relative motion between the weight and the frame of the seismometer, which is attached to the ground. The weight is often attached to a magnet which moves inside a coil of wire (Fig. 10.19). This set-up works according to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: the changing magnetic flux through the coil induces an emf in the coil, which gives rise to an induced electric current.

blocks.alt: A stand on a base plate with an overhead arm. A cylindrical weight hangs from the arm on a spring; a stylus from the weight touches a gridded recording drum standing on the base, on which a red wiggly trace is drawn.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.19: Seismometer (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.19).

blocks.text: The induced current is proportional to the velocity of the ground motion. The electrical signals generated are amplified and recorded, providing data on the amplitude, frequency and duration of the earthquake waves. The data are analysed to determine various characteristics of the earthquake, such as its location, magnitude and depth.

Usually a seismometer is buried under the ground at a depth of 50 to 1000 metres, in a protective case called a vault: a cylindrical steel tank approximately 1 metre wide and 2 metres deep, with a concrete pad at the bottom (Fig. 10.20). In the station of Fig. 10.20, solar energy charges the batteries, GPS gives the location, the seismic equipment in the vault transmits data, and a computer stores the data.

blocks.alt: A not-to-scale cross-section. Rings spread from an earthquake focus in the ground; a wave trace runs to seismic equipment in an underground vault. A mast above the vault carries a GPS antenna and a solar panel lit by the Sun, and a dashed link carries data to a computer. Labels: Not to scale!, Earthquake, Solar energy charges the batteries, GPS communicate with the satellites for location, Seismic equipment in vault transmits data to computer, Computer stores the data.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.20: A seismometer station: equipment in a vault, solar power, GPS and a computer (not to scale) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.20).

blocks.text: Most earthquakes are caused by plate tectonics (displacement). Those down to about 60 km deep are shallow, intermediate ones are as deep as 280 km beneath the crust, and deep earthquakes reach depths past 280 km (For Your Information). There are two main types of seismic waves: P-waves, the primary waves, which are longitudinal, and S-waves, the secondary waves, which are transverse in nature (For Your Information).
